summary: Defines how IP and ARP packets are transmitted over a Switched Multi-megabit Data Service network configured as a logical IP subnetwork. It is an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1209 explains how IP and ARP packets travel over the SMDS service when it is configured as a logical IP subnetwork. It specifies the packet headers, address resolution and maximum IP packet size.

subtitle: The packet format and address-resolution rules for sending IP and ARP over an SMDS logical subnet.

tldr.problem: IP hosts connected through SMDS need compatible rules for sending IP packets and resolving Internet addresses to SMDS addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC carries IP and ARP in LLC and SNAP headers over SMDS. It uses ARP for address resolution and sets the IP MTU to 9180 octets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1209 is an Internet Standard covering the logical IP subnetwork configuration. It does not define other public or inter-company configurations, and it does not discuss security issues.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1209 as an Internet Standard with no obsoleting or updating RFCs. The document covers the logical IP subnetwork configuration and leaves other SMDS configurations outside its scope.

sections.title: What SMDS Provides
sections.content:
Switched Multi-megabit Data Service (SMDS) is a public, connectionless, packet-switched data service. Each data unit is switched separately, without setting up a connection first. SMDS carries individual and group-addressed packets and can transfer up to 9188 octets of user information in one transmission.

SMDS addresses contain a 60-bit address and a 4-bit Address Type. The type identifies an individual or group address. RFC 1209 defines how directly connected IP stations and routers send IP and ARP over this service.
sections.plainLanguage: SMDS sends each data packet separately and supports individual and group addresses. This RFC defines how an IP station uses those features to send IP and ARP packets.

sections.title: The Logical IP Subnetwork
sections.content:
A logical IP subnetwork (LIS) is a group of stations configured to share an IP network or subnet number. Stations in one LIS communicate directly over SMDS. A station outside the LIS is reached through an IP router that belongs to both subnetworks.

Each LIS operates independently of other LISs on the same SMDS service. The RFC covers directly connected stations and routers, not MAC-level bridging. It leaves broader public and inter-company configurations to future documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Stations in the same LIS share an IP subnet and communicate directly. A router provides communication with stations in another subnet.

sections.title: Addresses Each Station Must Know
sections.content:
Each IP station must be configurable with its individual SMDS address, the LIS group address and the address where it sends ARP requests. In the initial LIS configuration, the ARP request address is the LIS group address. Each station accepts packets sent to its individual address and to the LIS group address.

A router connecting multiple LISs must support a separate set of these values for each connected LIS and associate each set with an IP network or subnet number. SMDS address-screening tables are not required for IP over SMDS. If used, they must allow communication among LIS members and use of the group address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each station needs its own SMDS address, the group's address and an address for ARP requests. A router joining LISs keeps a separate set of these values for each subnet.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Packet Size
sections.content:
IP and ARP packets are carried inside IEEE 802.2 LLC and SNAP headers, over the three-level SMDS Interface Protocol. The LLC and SNAP headers together use 8 octets. The SNAP EtherType identifies IP as 2048 (hexadecimal 0800) and ARP as 2054 (hexadecimal 0806). Multi-byte fields use big-endian order.

SMDS allows 9188 information octets in a transmission. After the LLC and SNAP headers, the IP MTU must be 9180 octets. The RFC defines no minimum packet size and prohibits trailer encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has LLC and SNAP headers that identify whether it carries IP or ARP. The largest IP packet allowed by this specification is 9180 octets.

sections.title: Using ARP to Find SMDS Addresses
sections.content:
Stations use Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) to map a 32-bit Internet address to an SMDS address. A host must know its own Internet and SMDS addresses, answer ARP requests and use ARP to find other hosts.

The SMDS hardware type in ARP is 14, the hardware address length is 8, and the IP protocol address length is 4. An ARP request goes to the configured ARP request address. In an LIS, that is normally the group's SMDS address, which delivers it to all LIS members.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP asks which SMDS address belongs to an IP address. In an LIS, the request is sent to the group address so the matching station can reply.

sections.title: Broadcast and Multicast Packets
sections.content:
SMDS does not provide complete hardware broadcast addressing. Therefore, the IP broadcast address for a network must map to the LIS group address. If IP multicast is supported, the RFC recommends mapping all multicast IP addresses to that same group address.

Because the group address does not support dynamic membership changes, each destination host must filter multicast packets and keep only the ones it needs. The RFC also requires compliant stations to support IEEE 802.2 Class I service, including some functions not directly used by IP and ARP.
sections.plainLanguage: IP broadcast and multicast use the LIS group address. Each host filters multicast packets because SMDS does not dynamically manage group membership.
